title: Why Do Traffic Jams Appear From Nowhere?
pause_note: 'long' lists beat indices followed by a pause; Short: 0.6 s

beats: Why do traffic jams appear from nowhere?
No crash. No roadworks. Nothing up ahead.
In a 2008 study in Japan, twenty-two cars drove around a ring, two hundred and thirty metres long.
Drivers held about thirty kilometres an hour. The road was crowded but clear.
Within minutes, a jam appeared anyway.
One driver eases off. The next reacts late, and brakes a little harder.
Each car passes it back, bigger, until cars almost stop.
So a jam is a wave. Cars move forward, but the jam slides backwards, at about twenty kilometres an hour.
That's why you crawl through a jam, and find nothing there.
